source_arguments.summary: Marcus accepts that rational, social beings should understand their social action, while disputing the move from that awareness to treating a good turn as a debt.
source_arguments.limits: This is an objection-and-reply. His assent to conscious social action is not agreement with every part of the objection about recognition.

source_arguments.summary: The vine bearing fruit explains the proposed attitude toward helping: perform the social function and continue, without making repayment what completes the act.
source_arguments.limits: This is an analogy and a functional view of human nature, not a demonstrated law about every practical situation.

source_arguments.summary: The revenge reminder directs the response away from imitation, but this short cited passage does not explain why that is the best revenge.
source_arguments.limits: No additional justification is attributed to Marcus here. A further reason would need another cited passage or an explicit editorial label.

source_arguments.summary: The bee/hive comparison presents individual and shared good as connected.
source_arguments.limits: The line supplies an analogy, not an argument that every demand by a community is just.

passages.text:
Such there be, who when they have done a good turn to any, are ready
to set them on the score for it, and to require retaliation. Others
there be, who though they stand not upon retaliation, to require any,
yet they think with themselves nevertheless, that such a one is their
debtor, and they know as their word is what they have done. Others again
there be, who when they have done any such thing, do not so much as
know what they have done; but are like unto the vine, which beareth her
grapes, and when once she hath borne her own proper fruit, is contented
and seeks for no further recompense. As a horse after a race, and a
hunting dog when he hath hunted, and a bee when she hath made her honey,
look not for applause and commendation; so neither doth that man that
rightly doth understand his own nature when he hath done a good turn:
but from one doth proceed to do another, even as the vine after she hath
once borne fruit in her own proper season, is ready for another time.
Thou therefore must be one of them, who what they do, barely do it
without any further thought, and are in a manner insensible of what they
do. 'Nay but,' will some reply perchance, 'this very thing a rational
man is bound unto, to understand what it is, that he doeth.' For it
is the property, say they, of one that is naturally sociable, to be
sensible, that he doth operate sociably: nay, and to desire, that the
party him self that is sociably dealt with, should be sensible of it
too. I answer, That which thou sayest is true indeed, but the true
meaning of that which is said, thou dost not understand. And therefore
art thou one of those first, whom I mentioned. For they also are led by
a probable appearance of reason. But if thou dost desire to understand
truly what it is that is said, fear not that thou shalt therefore give
over any sociable action.

revisions.text: Another person’s ingratitude does not release you from the work of cooperation. Respond without reproducing their wrongdoing; judge your response by what it contributes to shared life, rather than by the repayment it wins.

revisions.scope: Choosing a response after an unacknowledged favor or another person’s wrongdoing; a three-passage interpretation, not a rule about every conflict.
revisions.qualifications: This does not establish that every favor serves the common good, that harm must be endured, or that one must keep helping a dangerous person. These passages do not supply a complete rule for setting boundaries.
revisions.assumptions: Joins the no-repayment reminder, the non-imitation constraint and the hive analogy into one criterion for responding. No individual excerpt independently proves the whole conclusion.
revisions.practical_implication: Separate the wish to be repaid from what fair cooperation now requires. Concrete safety or boundary-setting tactics would be labeled modern applications and need their own review.

premises.claim: A good turn need not leave the recipient in your debt; the reminder still concerns conscious social action.
The reply to wrongdoing should not reproduce the wrongdoer’s character.
The individual’s good is connected to the shared community’s good.

synthesis.interpretive_step: The first passage removes repayment as the criterion of a good action. The second places a limit on a retaliatory response. The third supplies a social criterion. Together they suggest how to choose the next action after ingratitude: cooperation without imitation of wrongdoing.
synthesis.what_changes: Three separate reminders become one decision rule for a particular recurring situation. The sources do not themselves state this combined rule; that bridge is an editorial synthesis.
synthesis.not_claimed: This does not establish that every favor serves the common good, that harm must be endured, or that one must keep helping a dangerous person. These passages do not supply a complete rule for setting boundaries.
synthesis.expression_choice: “The kind of person your next act makes you” translates the response constraint into a question of character. It is editorial wording, not a quotation. The maxim is judged separately from fidelity.

revisions.text: Do not let another person’s failure decide the kind of person your next act makes you. Give what serves the shared life without turning generosity into a debt, or making a second wrong your answer to the first.

Read alongside the hive analogy and the instruction not to imitate wrongdoing, this suggests a practical test: what response serves our shared life without reproducing the wrong?
